title: MOSES BEFORE THE BURNING BUSH
paragraphs:
MOSES BEFORE THE BURNING BUSH
The Forty-Year Failure God Refused to Throw Away
There are moments in life when a person becomes haunted by a single question:
One failure that refuses to stay buried.
You imagine the life you could have lived if you had not made that choice.
You wonder whether God still has a future for someone carrying a past like yours.
If that question has ever lived inside your heart, then the story of Moses before the burning bush is not merely history.
Because before Moses became the great deliverer of Israel...
A man hiding in the wilderness.
A man whose greatest dreams seemed permanently destroyed.
And that is precisely where God met him.
Moses was born during a season of oppression when Pharaoh ordered Hebrew baby boys to be killed (Exodus 1:22).
The very child Pharaoh wanted dead was raised inside Pharaoh’s palace.
Even his name reflects divine providence.
Because Pharaoh’s daughter drew him out of the Nile (Exodus 2:10).
Everything about Moses’ life seemed destined for greatness.
“Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians and was powerful in his words and deeds.”
He had access to everything the world could offer.
Yet despite all his advantages, something deeper burned inside him.
One day Moses saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew slave.
So he struck the Egyptian and killed him.
Then he buried the body in the sand.
One failed attempt to accomplish God’s purpose through human strength.
The next day he discovered the truth.
And suddenly the prince became a criminal.
“When Pharaoh heard of this matter, he sought to kill Moses.”
Imagine replaying that day for years.
Moses probably believed his calling had ended before it ever began.
The man who thought he would rescue Israel became a shepherd in Midian.
Long enough to think God had forgotten.
Long enough to believe your best days are behind you.
Long enough for people to stop expecting anything from you.
Long enough to accept a smaller life.
Most people know Moses as the deliverer.
Few realize Moses spent far more years in obscurity than in public ministry.
But Scripture repeatedly reveals a different pattern.
Joseph had a prison before a palace.
David had caves before a crown.
Paul had years of obscurity before global ministry.
Jesus spent approximately thirty years in relative anonymity before three years of public ministry.
The wilderness often becomes His classroom.
Then one ordinary day changed history.
“Now Moses was tending the flock of Jethro his father-in-law.”
הַסְּנֶה בֹּעֵר בָּאֵשׁ וְהַסְּנֶה אֵינֶנּוּ אֻכָּל
“The bush was burning with fire, yet the bush was not consumed.”
The presence of God rested upon weakness without destroying it.
Because that bush resembles every believer.
Yet capable of carrying divine presence.
The God of heaven knew his name.
The God Moses thought had abandoned him had never stopped watching him.
The same God who saw him in Egypt saw him in Midian.
The same God who saw his failure saw his future.
The same God who saw his scandal saw his redemption.
Then came one of the most sacred declarations in Scripture:
Because holiness had invaded ordinary ground.
What changed was the presence of God.
A hospital room can become holy ground.
A prison cell can become holy ground.
A living room can become holy ground.
A place of tears can become holy ground.
When God enters a moment, everything changes.
The God who remains faithful when people fail.
The God who remains holy when cultures change.
The God who remains sovereign when circumstances collapse.
And then came the shocking announcement.
The one who had spent forty years believing his story was over.
“So now, go. I am sending you to Pharaoh to bring My people the Israelites out of Egypt.”
Can you imagine hearing those words?
The mission Moses ruined decades earlier was now being handed back to him.
Not because Moses had become impressive.
Not because Moses earned another chance.
But because grace had entered the story.
This is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
The Gospel is not primarily about good people becoming better.
It is about dead people receiving life.
It is about failures receiving mercy.
It is about sinners receiving forgiveness.
It is about God rewriting stories human beings believe are finished.
That theme reaches its fullest expression in Jesus Christ.
The same divine identity revealed at the burning bush echoes through Christ.
Moses delivered Israel from Egyptian slavery.
Jesus delivers humanity from slavery to sin.
At the cross, scandal met grace.
The greatest scandal in history became the greatest display of grace in history.
Perhaps that is why the story of Moses resonates so deeply.
Most of us are not afraid of hard work.
We are afraid our failures have disqualified us.
We fear that God can use other people but not us.
We secretly believe our worst chapter became the final chapter.
Yet Moses stands across history declaring otherwise.
Maybe your burning bush moment has not happened yet.
Maybe you are still in Midian.
Still carrying memories you wish you could erase.
Do not mistake silence for abandonment.
Do not mistake delay for rejection.
Do not mistake wilderness for disqualification.
The God who called Moses still calls people today.
The God who restored Moses still restores people today.
The God who rewrites stories still rewrites stories today.
And perhaps the greatest miracle was never the bush.
Perhaps the greatest miracle was that God looked at a broken man and said:
Maybe that is what your soul needed to hear today.
Not that your past is small.
Not that your mistakes never happened.
And Jesus still specializes in turning wildernesses into callings, failures into testimonies, and scandals into stories of redemption.
If you desire to glorify God through Gospel-centered outreach, your support becomes part of that mission.
The bush burned, but it was not consumed—just like the calling God placed on your life.
